title: Taken up (Assumption, 15 August)
hook: defined in 1950, Catholics hold Mary was taken body and soul into heavenly glory (CCC 966)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seven sorrows, from Simeon's prophecy to the tomb. Your line was a sword shall pierce thy soul. Were you gentle with someone's grief? Day eighty-two. After the sorrows, the end of Mary's story.

In much of Europe, the middle of August is when everything closes. In Italy it's called Ferragosto: shops shut, cities empty, families head to the beach. In France, Spain, Poland and plenty of other places, August fifteenth is a public holiday. Most tourists have no idea why. The reason is a feast of Mary, one of the oldest. And the Bible never describes the event it celebrates. Scripture doesn't tell us how Mary's life on earth ended. Not a word. So where does the feast come from, and why did a pope in 1950 make it a formal teaching of the faith? Today's word is the name of the feast.
screen: `FERRAGOSTO: EVERYTHING CLOSES.` → `A FEAST OF MARY.` → `THE BIBLE IS SILENT.`

segments.voice: On November first, 1950, Pope Pius the Twelfth defined it: Mary, when the course of her earthly life was finished, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory. Before he did, he wrote to bishops all over the world asking what their people believed. The answer was overwhelming. Christians had been celebrating this in some form for well over a thousand years. Notice the word. Jesus ascended: he went up by his own power. Mary was assumed, from the Latin for taken up. She didn't rise by herself. She was received. And notice what the definition leaves out. It doesn't say whether Mary died first. Most Catholics, and the long tradition, say she did. Eastern Christians call the same August feast the Dormition, the falling asleep of Mary. Catholics often point to a picture from the Book of Revelation, in the Douay-Rheims: "A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars." But the Church is honest that the teaching rests on tradition and the Church's faith, not one verse. Here's why it matters, and it's not only about Mary. The Catechism calls it a share in her son's resurrection and a preview of ours. Catholics say in the Creed that they believe in the resurrection of the body. Not escape from the body. The body, raised. The Assumption says that what God did for Jesus, he's already begun doing for one of us. Your body, with its knees and scars and tiredness, isn't a shell. It's part of you, and it's meant for glory.
screen: `NOVEMBER 1, 1950.` · `ASCENDED VS. ASSUMED.` · `THE DORMITION: FALLING ASLEEP.` · `A PREVIEW OF OUR RESURRECTION.` · then, large: `TAKEN UP BODY AND SOUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treat your body with care. Settle and breathe. Start at your feet and slowly move your attention up: legs, back, shoulders, hands, face. Notice where you're tired or sore or tight. Don't judge any of it. Just thank each part for carrying you today. Let your shoulders drop. If you pray, you can thank God for your body, as it is. If you don't, just be kind to it for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Assumption. From the Latin for taken up. Catholics hold Mary was taken body and soul into glory, a preview of the resurrection. Today's word.
Your line: the body matters. Today, do one kind thing for your body: water, a walk, sleep, a real meal. Day eighty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Assumption on 15 August, a holy day of obligation in many countries, and Eastern Christians keep the same day as the Dormition of the Mother of God.

original.note: Latin: a taking up, a receiving. from assumere, to take to oneself.

what a scholar hears: Munificentissimus Deus, 1950, leaves open whether she died first, and the East has kept the same day as the Dormition for centuries.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Revelation (Apocalypse) 12:1 given from memory; the DR book name is 'Apocalypse'. Confirm.
Munificentissimus Deus, 1 November 1950; Deiparae Virginis Mariae (1946) consulted the bishops. Confirm.
Feast 'well over a thousand years': the Dormition/Assumption feast was widespread by the 6th–7th centuries (Emperor Maurice fixed 15 August c. 600). Confirm.
'Most Catholics and the long tradition say she died': John Paul II (general audience, 25 June 1997) favored this view. Confirm phrasing.
Public holiday on 15 August in Italy, France, Spain, Poland and others. Confirm list.
'Taken up body and soul' in the teach screen paraphrases the definition; not presented as a quotation.
